conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling really nauseous and vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started this morning—really intense nausea and I’ve been vomiting green stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bilious vomiting. That’s consistent with your gastroparesis. You were just discharged two days ago—were you tolerating food then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips and crackers. I even ate a banana yesterday. But today it all came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re not able to keep any pills down either?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not even the Zofran or Reglan. I tried this morning but threw it up right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll give you IV fluids and anti-nausea meds to start. We also need to check your blood sugar and electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar’s usually okay with my Lantus at night. But I haven’t eaten, so it might be low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that closely. Also, I see you have a history of breathing problems with Ativan—anything over 0.25 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had apnea once in the ER after 1 mg. I only take half a tablet now if I must.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll avoid IV Ativan and be very cautious with dosing. For now, we’re giving Zofran IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your sodium dropped to 128 yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had low sodium before when I’m sick like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s likely due to SIADH from severe nausea. We’ve stopped IV fluids and put you on fluid restriction to help it rise safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t drink much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll recheck your sodium today and tomorrow. It’s already up to 131 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My stomach still feels full, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still attributing that to gastroparesis. Gastroenterology wants to do an endoscopy to make sure there’s no other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I had one a few months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but your symptoms are worsening and frequent. We need to rule out new problems like a blockage or worsening esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood and urine cultures came back negative. No infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a fever the first night—was that just from being dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature was actually low at one point—95.6. But your white count was high, so we checked for infection. It looks like stress from nausea caused the changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. Your vitals and labs are improving as your nausea settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray yesterday. Your lungs are clear, which supports that your low sodium is from SIADH, not a lung issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw something about a catheter in the report?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your port is visible, and the line is in good position. That’s how we’ve been giving your meds and drawing labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You just got back from your endoscopy. Everything looked okay in the stomach, but you do have esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation in the esophagus? Could that be making me nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can contribute, but it’s not the main cause. The good news is no ulcers or blockages. Biopsies confirmed mild inflammation, likely from reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on Protonix twice a day to treat the esophagitis. And we’re increasing your erythromycin to three times a day to help with stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought erythromycin was an antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At low doses, it acts as a stomach stimulant. It’s commonly used for gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is now 134—back in a safe range. We’re lifting the fluid restriction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting you on clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your gastric pacer was adjusted this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help? It hasn’t been changed in months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team thought it might need optimization. Since the adjustment, you’ve had less nausea and kept down apple juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been running high—around 160s over 90. We’ve been giving labetalol IV since you couldn’t take pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take lisinopril and a clonidine patch at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your lisinopril and increased it to 10 mg daily. The clonidine patch was discontinued—it can worsen nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a known side effect. We’ll monitor your BP. You’ll need a blood test—chem-7—before seeing your PCP next week to check your potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re tolerating solid food, your sodium is stable, and your BP is in the 130s over 80.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home on your regular insulin, Reglan, Zofran, and compazine suppositories. Erythromycin three times a day and Protonix twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take half a tablet as needed, but be cautious. If you feel drowsy or short of breath, stop and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my GI appointment tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. ___ to review the pacer settings and your progress. And see your PCP next week for BP follow-up and the blood test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if this happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can’t keep fluids down for more than 12 hours, or have dizziness, chest pain, or trouble breathing, come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll try to stick to small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And keep using your anti-nausea meds early. We’re discharging you in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this round wasn’t as bad as the last one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We caught it early, adjusted your pacer, and treated the esophagitis. That should help prevent frequent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. Ten times in three months is too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. Take care, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.
